pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that cluster on new growth, buds, and the undersides of leaves, leaving sticky honeydew and curled leaves. Calendula is a known aphid magnet. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and the flowers also draw in ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Calendula is notably attractive to aphids and is sometimes grown as a deliberate trap or banker plant. Soft-bodied sap-feeders colonize tender growth and buds, secreting honeydew and occasionally vectoring viruses. Usually held in check by the beneficial predators the flowers recruit; hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.

pests.name: Whiteflies
pests.note_beginner: Small white flying insects that hide and feed on the undersides of leaves and fly up in a cloud when disturbed. Knock them back with a hard stream of water or insecticidal soap, and check leaf undersides regularly.
pests.note_seasoned: Tiny white sap-feeders that congregate on lower leaf surfaces, producing honeydew and sooty mold; calendula is a frequent host. Manage with strong water sprays, insecticidal soap, and removal of heavily infested lower leaves; yellow sticky cards help monitor.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and young plants, especially in the cool, damp weather calendula likes and on tender seedlings. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding spots, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Ragged feeding on seedlings and lower foliage in the cool, moist conditions calendula favors; young plantings are a frequent target. Reduce mulch harborage, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait, and avoid overhead watering late in the day.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery film on leaves, most common in warm, humid weather, crowded plantings, and as summer heat arrives. It is calendula's main disease and a sign the season is turning too warm for it. Space plants for airflow, water at the soil, plant in full sun, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Calendula's signature disease, worsening as warm, humid weather and summer heat set in, which is also when the cool-season plant naturally declines. Favored by crowding, shade, and overhead wetness. Manage culturally with full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and sanitation; in mild and Mediterranean zones it is least troublesome in the cool months and worst in the warm shoulder.

diseases.name: Damping-off and root or stem rot
diseases.note_beginner: Wet, poorly drained soil rots roots and stem bases, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line, especially in cold, soggy soil. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and avoid sowing into cold, waterlogged ground.
diseases.note_seasoned: Soilborne rots and seedling damping-off driven by cold, wet, poorly drained soil, the standing risk for a cool-season plant grown through damp weather. Prevent with well-drained soil, restrained watering, and good airflow rather than treatment; do not sow into waterlogged ground.

diseases.name: Cucumber mosaic and aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: Less common problems spread by insects: a mosaic virus carried by aphids that mottles and distorts leaves, and aster yellows, spread by leafhoppers, which yellows and deforms growth. There is no cure; remove and discard affected plants and manage the insects that spread them.
diseases.note_seasoned: Occasional insect-vectored problems: cucumber mosaic virus (aphid-transmitted, causing mottling and distortion) and aster yellows phytoplasma (leafhopper-vectored, causing chlorosis and virescent, greened blooms across the aster family). No cure; rogue out symptomatic plants and manage aphids, leafhoppers, and nearby weed reservoirs.
